items.new: Squeeze! Squeeze! Squeeze! All the morning long I squeezed that sperm till I myself almost melted into it. I squeezed that sperm till a strange sort of madness came over me, and I found myself unwittingly squeezing my co-workers' hands in it, mistaking their hands for the gentle globules. Such an overflowing, affectionate, friendly, loving feeling did this work beget that at last I was continually squeezing their hands and looking up into their eyes sentimentally — as much as to say: Oh, my dear fellow beings, why should we any longer harbor any social bitterness, or know the slightest ill-humor or envy! Come, let us squeeze hands all round. No, let us all squeeze ourselves into each other. Let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.

items.new: There is another substance, a very singular one, which turns up in the course of this business, but which I find very difficult to adequately describe. It is called slobgollion — a name original with the whalemen, and the substance itself is just as original. It is an indescribably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm after a prolonged squeezing and subsequent decanting. I hold it to be the wondrously thin, ruptured membranes of the case, fused together.

items.new: Look at the sailor called the mincer, who now comes along and, assisted by two helpers, heavily shoulders the grandissimus, as the mariners call it, and with bowed shoulders staggers off with it as if he were a grenadier carrying a dead comrade from the field. Laying it upon the forecastle deck, he proceeds to remove its dark skin cylindrically, as an African hunter skins a boa. This done, he turns the skin inside out like a trouser leg, gives it a good stretching so as almost to double its diameter, and at last hangs it, well spread, in the rigging to dry. Before long it is taken down. Removing some three feet from the pointed end and then cutting two slits for armholes at the other end, he lengthwise slips himself bodily into it. The mincer now stands before you invested in the full canonicals (the clerical vestments) of his calling. As it has for all his order from time immemorial, this investiture alone will adequately protect him while employed in the peculiar functions of his office.

items.new: Nevertheless, the sun does not hide Virginia's Dismal Swamp, nor Rome's accursed Campagna, nor the wide Sahara, nor all the millions of miles of deserts and of griefs beneath the moon. The sun does not hide the ocean, which is the dark side of this earth, and which is two-thirds of this earth. So therefore, that mortal man who has more of joy than sorrow in him — that mortal man cannot be true — not true, or undeveloped. With books the same. The truest of all men was the Man of Sorrows, and the truest of all books is Solomon's, and Ecclesiastes is the fine hammered steel of woe. "All is vanity." ALL. This willful world has not yet grasped unchristian Solomon's wisdom. But he who dodges hospitals and jails and walks fast crossing graveyards and would rather talk of operas than hell — who calls Cowper, Young, Pascal, Rousseau poor devils, all of them sick men, and throughout a carefree lifetime swears by Rabelais as supremely wise and therefore jolly — not that man is fitted to sit down on tombstones and break the green damp mold with the unfathomably wondrous Solomon.

items.new: See with what perfect freedom the whaleman takes his handful of lamps — often only old bottles and vials, though — to the copper cooler at the try-works and refills them there, as mugs of ale at a vat. He burns, too, the purest of oil, in its unprocessed and therefore untainted state — a fluid unknown to solar, lunar, or astral lamps on shore. It is sweet as early grass butter in April. He goes and hunts for his oil, so as to be sure of its freshness and genuineness, even as the traveler on the prairie hunts up his own supper of game.

items.new: In the sperm fishery, this is perhaps one of the most remarkable incidents in all the business of whaling. One day the planks stream with torrents of blood and oil. On the sacred quarter-deck, enormous masses of the whale's head are profanely piled. Great rusty casks lie about, as in a brewery yard. The smoke from the try-works has blackened all the bulwarks. The sailors go about coated with grease. The entire ship seems the great leviathan himself. And on all hands the noise is deafening.

items.new: But look: aloft there, at the three mastheads, stand three men intent on spotting more whales, which, if caught, will infallibly again soil the old oaken furniture and drop at least one small grease-spot somewhere. Yes — and many is the time when, after the severest uninterrupted labors that know no night, continuing straight through for ninety-six hours, when from the boat where they have swollen their wrists with all-day rowing on the equator, they only step to the deck to carry vast chains and heave the heavy windlass and cut and slash — yes, and in their very sweating to be smoked and burned anew by the combined fires of the equatorial sun and the equatorial try-works — when, on the heels of all this, they have finally roused themselves to clean the ship and make a spotless dairy room of it — many is the time the poor fellows, just buttoning the necks of their clean shirts, are startled by the cry of "There she blows!" And away they fly to fight another whale and go through the whole weary thing again. Oh, my friends, but this is man-killing! Yet this is life. For hardly have we mortals by long toiling extracted from this world's vast bulk its small but valuable sperm, and then with weary patience cleaned ourselves from its defilements and learned to live here in clean tabernacles of the soul — hardly is this done when: There she blows! The ghost is spouted up, and away we sail to fight some other world and go through young life's old routine again.

items.new: It has already been told how Ahab was in the habit of pacing his quarter-deck, taking regular turns between the binnacle and the mainmast. But in the multitude of other things requiring narration, it has not been added how sometimes in these walks, when most sunk in his mood, he would pause at each spot in turn and stand there strangely eyeing the particular object before him. When he halted before the binnacle, with his gaze fastened on the pointed needle in the compass, that glance shot like a javelin with the pointed intensity of his purpose. And when, resuming his walk, he again paused before the mainmast — then, as the same riveted gaze fastened upon the riveted gold coin there, he still wore the same expression of nailed firmness, only touched with a certain wild longing, if not hopefulness.

items.new: Now this doubloon was of purest, virgin gold, raked somewhere out of the heart of gorgeous hills, from which, east and west, over golden sands, the headwaters of many a Pactolus (the gold-bearing river of legend) flow. And though now nailed amid all the rustiness of iron bolts and the green tarnish of copper spikes, yet untouchable and immaculate to any filth, it still preserved its Quito glow. And though placed among a ruthless crew and every hour passed by ruthless hands, and through the livelong nights shrouded in thick darkness that might cover any pilfering approach — nevertheless, every sunrise found the doubloon where the sunset left it last. For it was set apart and sanctified to one awe-striking end. And however wild in their sailor ways, one and all, the mariners revered it as the white whale's talisman. Sometimes they talked it over in the weary night watch, wondering whose it was to be at last, and whether he would ever live to spend it.

items.new: Before the English ship fades from sight, let it be set down here that she hailed from London and was named after the late Samuel Enderby, merchant of that city, the founder of the famous whaling house of Enderby & Sons — a house which, in my poor whaleman's opinion, comes not far behind the united royal houses of the Tudors and Bourbons in terms of real historical interest. How long before the year 1775 this great whaling house existed, my numerous fish-documents do not make clear. But in that year it fitted out the first English ships that ever regularly hunted the sperm whale — though for some twenty years before that, ever since 1726, our valiant Coffins and Maceys of Nantucket and the Vineyard had in large fleets pursued that Leviathan, but only in the North and South Atlantic, not elsewhere. Let it be distinctly recorded here that the Nantucketers were the first among mankind to harpoon with civilized steel the great sperm whale, and that for half a century they were the only people of the whole globe who did so.

items.new: In 1778, a fine ship, the Amelia, fitted out for the express purpose and at the sole expense of the vigorous Enderbys, boldly rounded Cape Horn and was the first among the nations to lower a whaleboat of any sort in the great South Sea. The voyage was a skillful and lucky one, and returning to her berth with a full hold of precious sperm, the Amelia's example was soon followed by other ships, English and American, and thus the vast sperm whale grounds of the Pacific were thrown open. But not content with this good deed, the tireless house bestirred itself again. It was Samuel and all his sons — how many, only their mother knows — under whose immediate sponsorship, and partly, I think, at whose expense, the British government was induced to send the sloop-of-war Rattler on a whaling voyage of discovery into the South Sea. Commanded by a naval post-captain, the Rattler made a rattling voyage of it and did some service — how much does not appear. But this is not all. In 1819, the same house fitted out a discovery whale-ship of their own to go on a tasting cruise to the remote waters of Japan. That ship — well called the Syren — made a noble experimental cruise, and it was thus that the great Japanese whaling ground first became generally known. The Syren on this famous voyage was commanded by a Captain Coffin, a Nantucketer.

items.new: The beef was fine — tough but with body in it. They said it was bull-beef; others, that it was dromedary beef. But I do not know for certain which it was. They had dumplings too — small but substantial, symmetrically globular, and indestructible dumplings. I fancied that you could feel them and roll them about inside you after they were swallowed. If you stooped over too far forward, you risked their pitching out of you like billiard balls. The bread — but that couldn't be helped; besides, it was an anti-scorbutic (a guard against scurvy); in short, the bread contained the only fresh fare they had. But the forecastle was not very bright, and it was very easy to step into a dark corner when you ate it. But all in all, taking her from truck to helm, considering the dimensions of the cook's boilers, including his own live parchment boilers — fore and aft, I say, the Samuel Enderby was a jolly ship: of good food and plenty, fine flip and strong, crack fellows all, and capital from boot heels to hat-band.

During my research into the Leviathanic histories, I stumbled upon an ancient Dutch volume which, by the musty whaling smell of it, I knew must be about whalers. The title was "Dan Coopman," so I concluded that this must be the invaluable memoirs of some Amsterdam cooper in the fishery, as every whale-ship must carry its cooper. I was supported in this belief by seeing that it was written by one "Fitz Swackhammer." But my friend Dr. Snodhead, a very learned man, professor of Low Dutch and High German at the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott's, to whom I handed the work for translation, giving him a box of sperm candles for his trouble — this same Dr. Snodhead, as soon as he saw the book, assured me that "Dan Coopman" did not mean "The Cooper" but "The Merchant." In short, this ancient and learned Low Dutch book treated of the commerce of Holland, and among other subjects contained a very interesting account of its whale fishery. And in this chapter, headed "Smeer," or "Fat," I found a long, detailed list of the provisions for the larders and cellars of 180 Dutch whalers.
